title: Feasibility and quantitative performance of dissonance/novelty classification using simple model-derived features
content: It is possible to classify an input factual statement $X$ into three mutually exclusive categories—Novel, Familiar, and Dissonant—using lightweight features derived from model inner states (per-layer activation statistics and gradient statistics) and from model outputs. Using simple classifiers (Support Vector Machines and Random Forests) with combined activation-and-gradient features (A+G) yields high accuracy: for a GPT-2 model fine-tuned on 1000 known facts, SVM (A+G, historical (layer-wise cumulative) normalization) achieves 0.995 (±0.001) accuracy, and RF (A+G, raw) achieves 0.988 (±0.001); for a pre-trained GPT-2 model the best results are SVM (A+G, historical) 0.947 (±0.004) and RF (A+G, raw) 0.928 (±0.012). These results demonstrate that readily-extractable statistics (mean, std, min, max, quartiles) of activations and gradients or output-only probability features contain strong, deployable signatures that discriminate between novel, familiar, and dissonant facts.

title: Definition and operational collection of historical neuron usage metrics
content:
A concrete, operational scheme for accumulating and normalizing historical neuron usage is defined and implemented. For each neuron index $n$ (across transformer blocks and projection matrices), the pipeline accumulates per-step raw activations $A^l(t)$ and gradients $G^l(t)$ at layer $l$ and training step $t$. These are standardized per layer using the mean and standard deviation over all dimensions:
      $$
      \hat{A}^l(t)=\frac{A^l(t)-\mu^l_A(t)}{\sigma^l_A(t)},\quad \hat{G}^l(t)=\frac{G^l(t)-\mu^l_G(t)}{\sigma^l_G(t)},
      $$
      where $\mu^l_A(t)$ and $\sigma^l_A(t)$ are the mean and standard deviation of $A^l(t)$, and similarly for $G^l(t)$. The standardized values are summed over the batch dimension and optionally over token positions to obtain per-step sums $S^l_{\hat{A}}(t)_i$ and $S^l_{\hat{G}}(t)_i$ for each neuron $i$. These per-step sums are then accumulated across all training steps $T$ to form cumulative historical measures:
      $$
      H\hat{A}^l_i=\sum_{t=1}^T S^l_{\hat{A}}(t)_i,\quad H\hat{G}^l_i=\sum_{t=1}^T S^l_{\hat{G}}(t)_i.
      $$
      These historical aggregates enable ranking neurons by past usage and serve both (i) layer-wise normalization for the dissonance classifier and (ii) selection criteria for targeted updates.

title: A practical neuron-specific gradient-masking update mechanism and four neuron-selection strategies
content: A simple, implementable targeted-update mechanism is proposed and exercised: during training on new facts, compute standard forward/backward gradients and then zero-out (mask) gradients for parameters that do not belong to a chosen neuron set, so only selected neurons and their associated weights are updated by the optimizer. Four concrete neuron-selection strategies are specified, where $H\hat{G}_n$ is the historical gradient magnitude for neuron $n$ (cumulative standardized gradient sum over training), $G_n^\text{new}$ is the gradient magnitude from a single backpropagation pass on the new data, $|\mathcal{N}|$ is the total number of neurons, and $N$ is the number of selected neurons: (a) Plastic neurons: $\mathcal{N}_{\text{plastic}}=\{n\mid \mathrm{rank}(H\hat{G}_n)\le N\}$ selecting neurons with lowest historical gradient magnitude; (b) Stubborn neurons: $\mathcal{N}_{\text{stubborn}}=\{n\mid \mathrm{rank}(H\hat{G}_n)>|\mathcal{N}|-N\}$ selecting highest historical gradient magnitudes; (c) Candidate neurons: $\mathcal{N}_{\text{candidate}}=\{n\mid \mathrm{rank}(G_n^\text{new})>|\mathcal{N}|-N\}$; and (d) Specific neurons: $\mathcal{N}_{\text{specific}}=\text{Top}_N(\mathcal{N}_\text{all}\setminus\mathcal{N}_\text{stubborn})$ selecting high-$G^\text{new}$ neurons that explicitly avoid stubborn neurons, where $\mathcal{N}_\text{all}$ is the set of all neurons. This gradient-masking workflow is computationally lightweight and directly controls where parameter updates are applied.

title: Non-dissonant updates tend to preserve unrelated prior knowledge; tradeoffs among targeting strategies
content: In experiments that add non-dissonant (non-contradictory) facts after training on an initial set of 2000 facts from the COUNTERFACT dataset, GPT-2-small shows strong inherent robustness to preserving unrelated prior knowledge under many update modes. Empirical observations indicate that full fine-tuning (updating all parameters) reduces old-fact accuracy on the 2000 tracked facts from near-100% to approximately 93%, whereas updating plastic neurons preserves old-fact accuracy above 98% (for neuron budgets up to 20,000 neurons). Plastic-neuron updates require more neurons or training time to reach high accuracy on the new facts; candidate, stubborn, or specific-neuron strategies learn new facts using fewer parameters but incur more degradation to tracked old facts. Thus, there is a tradeoff: avoiding heavily-used (stubborn) neurons improves retention of unrelated knowledge (stability) while some subnetworks (stubborn/candidate) enable efficient ingestion (plasticity).

title: Dissonant (contradictory) updates are catastrophically destructive to unrelated knowledge across models and strategies
content: Controlled experiments reveal that introducing dissonant updates—new data that directly contradicts previously learned associations—causes severe, widespread degradation of unrelated prior knowledge (measured on 2000 tracked facts from the COUNTERFACT dataset) regardless of model scale (GPT-2-small, GPT-2-xl, GPT-J-6B) and regardless of neuron-targeting strategy. Quantitatively, dissonant updates can drive old-fact accuracy well below 60% and, in some settings, below 40% even when editing as few as 10–100 contradictory facts; the destructive effect persists when editing 1,000 facts. This catastrophic interference occurs even when updates are restricted to neurons classified as plastic (rarely used) and also manifests on larger models that have greater capacity but still exhibit significant degradation of tracked unrelated facts.

title: Combining activation and gradient features improves dissonance detection; normalization effects and classifier choices characterized
content: Combining per-layer activation statistics and gradient statistics (A+G) yields consistently better classification performance than using either feature type alone. In the finetuned scenario (GPT-2 model fine-tuned on 1000 known facts), gradient-based features dominate feature importance; in the pre-trained scenario (pre-trained GPT-2 model), both activations and gradients contribute substantially. Historical (layer-wise cumulative) normalization helps SVM classifiers more than Random Forests in some settings. These feature-combination and normalization behaviors were validated through ablation in a cross-validated grid.

title: Model-output-only features achieve comparable dissonance-awareness performance
content: Features extracted solely from model outputs—conditional joint and truncated-token probabilities, top-100 next-token distributions, and 100-bin histogram summaries of per-token output distributions—can achieve dissonance/novelty classification performance comparable to internal-state features. In experiments on GPT-2-small, a concatenated output-feature set (1204 dimensions) achieved accuracy 0.983 on a pre-trained GPT-2 model and 0.978 on a GPT-2 model fine-tuned on 1000 known facts on the three-way classification task (Novel, Familiar, Dissonant), demonstrating that output-only detectors are a viable, lower-instrumentation alternative.

title: Empirical localization patterns: stubborn neurons concentrate in particular transformer blocks and attention matrices
content: Analysis of the historical-gradient distributions across transformer blocks of GPT-2-XL reveals non-uniform localization: neurons identified as stubborn (high historical gradient magnitude $H\hat{G}_n$) concentrate in certain blocks (not uniformly distributed), with the concatenated query, key, value attention matrix ($\text{Attn}_{\text{c_attn}}$) generally containing a larger share of stubborn neurons except in early blocks where the attention output projection matrix ($\text{Attn}_{\text{c_proj}}$) can dominate. Histograms across thresholds for defining stubborn neurons (e.g., top 2000 vs top 8000 neurons) confirm this block-level asymmetry.

title: Evidence that certain subnetworks (lottery-ticket-like neurons) preferentially support new-fact integration
content: Experiments that first trained a GPT-2-small model on 10,000 disjoint facts (Facts H) to identify highly active 'Lottery Ticket Neurons' (neurons with highest gradient magnitude $G_n^\text{new}$ from a single backpropagation pass on Facts H) and then restricted learning of different new facts (Facts A) to various neuron subsets show that the Lottery Ticket Neurons achieve substantially better new-fact acquisition with fewer neurons (e.g., approaching near-100% accuracy around 8,000 neurons) than non-lottery neurons (neurons underutilized during training on Facts H) or randomly selected neurons. This supports an extension of the lottery ticket hypothesis to factual integration in transformers: certain pre-existing subnetworks are more conducive to packing new factual associations.

title: Under multi-fact, contradiction-bearing conditions, candidate/specific neuron targeting can outperform some editing baselines but still fail to prevent catastrophic effects of dissonant updates
content: When benchmarked under multi-fact editing scenarios with 10, 100, and 1000 dissonant facts, candidate- and specific-neuron targeted-update strategies can achieve higher harmonic means (balancing old unrelated accuracy, new reliability, and generalization) than single-edit-focused editing methods such as ROME (Rank-One Model Editing) and MEMIT (Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer) in some multi-fact settings; however, no targeted strategy studied avoids the fundamental catastrophic interference produced by dissonant updates. The targeted strategies trade off differently along the preservation–ingestion Pareto front and occasionally outperform editing baselines on combined metrics, but none solve the dissonance-induced destruction problem.
